description: Learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

cards.title: Your Attachment Style Is Running the Show
cards.subtitle: Same fight. Different partner. Third time this year.
body: The relationship ends and you're convinced they were the problem. Then the next one unravels the exact same way.
You're three relationships in before you realize the script is yours.
cards.takeaway: Different partners, same ending—the common variable is you.

cards.title: Anxious, Avoidant, Secure—Know Which One You Are
cards.subtitle: They didn't text back for two hours. You've already written the breakup speech.
body: Anxious: you check your phone seventeen times before lunch. Avoidant: you feel suffocated when they want to see you three nights in a row.
Half the population is secure, a quarter anxious, a quarter avoidant.
cards.takeaway: Your style explains your behavior in ways your explanations can't.

cards.title: Neediness Is Not a Weakness
cards.subtitle: You apologized for needing them. They're the person you're dating.
body: You want reassurance after a bad day and immediately feel pathetic. The culture says you should be complete alone.
Partners regulate each other's heart rate, cortisol, immune function. Dependency and enmeshment are not the same thing.
cards.takeaway: We're biologically designed to co-regulate with another human.

cards.title: Avoidant People Aren't Cold—They're Defended
cards.subtitle: They said they needed space. What they meant was they needed armor.
body: Avoidant people feel everything—they just learned early that closeness ends badly. So they built walls.
The distance looks like confidence. It's actually protection.
cards.takeaway: The wall keeps pain out. It also keeps connection out.

cards.title: Protest Behavior Is a Signal, Not a Strategy
cards.subtitle: You called six times, sent twelve texts, and threatened to leave. You don't know why.
body: Excessive calling. Keeping score. Manufacturing jealousy. It's not a plan—it's an alarm system.
Your nervous system detected disconnection and started screaming.
cards.takeaway: Protest behavior is an alarm, not a strategy.

cards.title: The Anxious-Avoidant Trap Is the Most Common Drama
cards.subtitle: You chase. They pull back. You chase harder. They disappear.
body: Anxious pursues. Avoidant withdraws. The more you reach, the more they retreat.

• Both fears confirmed
• Most common dysfunctional pairing
• Both re-traumatize each other on autopilot
cards.takeaway: Someone has to see the loop before it stops.

cards.title: Secure People Make Everything Easier
cards.subtitle: They texted back in twenty minutes. You're bored. That's the problem.
body: Secure people are consistent. They show up. They don't create mystery or drama. And if you're anxious, that feels flat.
The intensity you think is passion is just your alarm system firing.
cards.takeaway: The absence of panic is not the absence of love.

cards.title: Effective Communication and Availability Are the Foundation
cards.subtitle: 'You never call me' starts a fight. 'I feel anxious when I don't hear from you' ends one.
body: Say what you need, not what they failed to do. No blame, no subtext, no test.
But communication only works if the other person is available. Availability isn't grand gestures—it's answering the text.
cards.takeaway: Secure people are available—that's the whole point.

cards.title: Dependency Is Not the Opposite of Independence
cards.subtitle: She's out climbing mountains alone. She's also the one who texts her partner every night.
body: Secure people take the biggest risks because their attachment base is solid.
Anxious people look needy because they're starving. Avoidant people avoid commitment entirely.
cards.takeaway: True independence requires a secure base, not isolation.

cards.title: Your Nervous System Picks Partners Before Your Brain Does
cards.subtitle: The chemistry was instant. So was the pattern you've been repeating for five years.
body: That electric spark you felt on date one isn't love—it's your nervous system recognizing someone who'll trigger you.

• Familiarity registers as attraction
• Anxious people mistake alarm bells for chemistry
cards.takeaway: If every relationship ends the same way, you're the common variable.

cards.title: Deactivating Strategies Look Like Strength
cards.subtitle: 'I don't need anyone.' It sounds confident. It's actually terrified.
body: Society rewards avoidant behavior. Fierce independence. Refusing to be needy. Quick exits.
But if it's driven by fear rather than choice, it's just armor with better branding.
cards.takeaway: Independence driven by fear is just dressed-up avoidance.

cards.title: Activating Strategies Look Like Overreaction
cards.subtitle: They took four hours to respond. You've already drafted three breakup scenarios.
body: When the anxious attachment system fires, threat detection goes nuclear. Every text gets analyzed.
It looks insane. It's not rational—it's biological.
cards.takeaway: Shaming someone for it makes the panic worse.

cards.title: The Fantasy of the Phantom Ex
cards.subtitle: Your current partner is great. Your ex from five years ago was better. Somehow.
body: The phantom ex lives in your head as the perfect one who got away. By keeping that fantasy alive, no current partner measures up.
It's a deactivating strategy with nostalgia as the excuse.
cards.takeaway: If every new person loses to a ghost, the ghost is the weapon.

cards.title: Attachment Shows Up Everywhere, Not Just Romance
cards.subtitle: Your friend cancels plans last minute. Again. You're more hurt than angry.
body: Attachment theory shapes how you show up with friends, family, and coworkers.
The anxious friend checks in constantly. The avoidant coworker keeps interactions surface-level.
cards.takeaway: It's not about this specific person—it's about your wiring.

cards.title: You Can Earn Security Over Time
cards.subtitle: Six months with them, you stopped checking your phone every ten minutes.
body: Anxious with a secure partner. Gradually you calm down. Avoidant with someone patient. Slowly you let them in.
Attachment styles shift—slowly, but they shift.
cards.takeaway: The fact that it's changeable is the only hopeful part of this research.

cards.title: Distance Is Not Space—It's Avoidance in Disguise
cards.subtitle: You had three great days in a row. Now they need a week alone.
body: Needing space is healthy. Needing distance every single time closeness increases is a pattern.
Healthy space has a return time. Avoidant distance has no plan to come back.
cards.takeaway: If distance always follows connection, it's not rest—it's defense.

cards.title: Dating Advice Often Rewards Avoidance
cards.subtitle: 'Wait three hours to text back.' 'Don't seem too interested.' Congrats, you're training yourself to be avoidant.
body: Dating culture treats unavailability as attractive and availability as desperate.

• Playing it cool is performing avoidance
• Vulnerability builds connection, mystery kills it
cards.takeaway: Most dating rules are a manual for insecure attachment.

cards.title: The Right Partner Calms Your Nervous System
cards.subtitle: You stopped checking your phone forty times a day. That's how you knew it was working.
body: A secure relationship doesn't feel like a rollercoaster. It feels like exhaling. Your nervous system shuts off the alarms.
You have energy for the rest of your life because you're not burning it on relationship panic.
cards.takeaway: The goal isn't excitement—it's calm.

cards.title: Conflict Isn't Failure—Withdrawal Is
cards.subtitle: You fought for two hours last night. This morning they won't speak to you.
body: Secure couples fight. They yell, they disagree, they work through it. What they don't do is stonewall.
The argument isn't the problem—disappearing afterward is.
cards.takeaway: Stonewalling does more damage than the fight itself.

cards.title: Love Is a Regulation System
cards.subtitle: Your blood pressure drops when they walk in the room. That's not poetry—that's biology.
body: Love isn't just emotion—it's a regulatory system. Your partner's presence affects your cortisol, immune function, heart rate.

• We co-regulate each other at the biological level
• The quality of your attachment affects your physical health
cards.takeaway: Treating it as biology, not just feelings, changes how you think about relationships.
